verdicts.corrected_claim: On the Pi 5 with the Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm kernel 6.12.96+rpt-rpi-2712 (2712 and v8 flavours, dated 2026-07-24), /dev/gpiochip0 is missing. In all three forum reports pinctrl-rp1 (54 lines) is gpiochip15, and gpiochip11–14 are the gpio-brcmstb SoC controllers. No report puts the header on gpiochip11. The udev rule 60-gpiochip4.rules matches only KERNEL=="gpiochip0", so the /dev/gpiochip4 compatibility symlink disappears as well. 6.12.93 (Bookworm) and 6.18.34 (Trixie) still show pinctrl-rp1 as gpiochip0. One user got gpiochip0 back by running rpi-update, which moved the kernel to 6.18.40. That is not an apt fix. No Raspberry Pi engineer has acknowledged the problem in either thread. The rpi-6.12.y source at 6.12.112 still contains the suspect code, so later Bookworm apt kernels are probably still affected (not verified on hardware). Any configuration or code that names a fixed chip number breaks: a static `--device /dev/gpiochip0` (or gpiochip4), and also native gpiozero/lgpio.
verdicts.evidence:
https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?p=2384025 ('pinctrl-rp1 no longer gpiochip0 with 6.12.96+rpt-rpi on bookworm'):

- neilgl, 2026-07-31: on 6.12.96 (2026-07-24), gpiochip11–14 are gpio-brcmstb and 'gpiochip15 [pinctrl-rp1] (54 lines)'; on 6.18.34 Trixie it is 'gpiochip0 [pinctrl-rp1]'.
https://forums.raspberrypi.com/viewtopic.php?p=2384297 ('All my GPIOs seem to have gone away', tomc42, 2026-07-31): pinctrl-rp1 is gpiochip15 with no gpiochip0 and lgpio falls back; after rpi-update to 6.18.40-v8-16k+, 'My GPIOs are back!'. No engineer replied in either thread.
Allsky PR https://github.com/AllskyTeam/allsky/pull/5340 lists the same numbering: brcmstb 11–14, pinctrl-rp1 15.
Source: raspberrypi/linux rpi-6.12.y drivers/gpio/gpiolib.c (Makefile SUBLEVEL 112) calls of_alias_get_id(gdev->dev.of_node, "gpiochip") at line 999, before device_set_node(... gpiochip_choose_fwnode(gc)) at line 1030. rpi-6.18.y uses of_alias_get_id(to_of_node(gpiochip_choose_fwnode(gc)), ...) at line 1100.
WLAN Pi PR https://github.com/WLAN-Pi/wlanpi-fpms/pull/192 (2026-09-25): on its own non-Raspberry-Pi-OS 7.1.13 / 7.2.7-2712 kernel the Pi 5 RP1 header is also gpiochip15. So chip numbers are not stable outside Raspberry Pi OS either.

verdicts.corrected_claim:
--privileged is not needed for GPIO through lgpio, but --device plus the gpio GID is not quite enough. In lgpio's C sources the only device path used for GPIO is /dev/gpiochip%d, opened O_RDWR and driven through the GPIO v2 uAPI (GPIO_V2_GET_LINE_IOCTL). There is no /dev/mem, /dev/gpiomem or sysfs GPIO access. A non-root container additionally needs a writable working directory, or LG_WD, for the notify FIFO that lgpio creates at import (see C21). gpiozero also needs /proc/cpuinfo to detect the board (C15). Precedents:
- The 2026 linux-voice-assistant example runs as user 1000:1000 with numeric group_add GIDs (GPIO_GID default 986), builds lg v0.2.2 from source and does `chmod a+w /app`. It was tested on a Pi Zero 2 W and a Pi 3, not a Pi 5, and its device mapping and privileged settings could not be seen in the diff.
- The libgpiod example in gpiozero discussion #1117 (Feb 2024, Pi 5) used `--device /dev/gpiochip4` without --privileged. The Alpine/py3-libgpiod Dockerfile in that thread also used gpiochip4 (2024 numbering) and did not state its run flags. No comment there shows `--device /dev/gpiochip0` alone.

verdicts.corrected_claim:
liblgpio / python3-lgpio are not in Debian's archive (no 'lgpio' or 'lg' source package; madison returns nothing). A plain Debian image therefore cannot apt-install them from Debian mirrors. Building from source (as the 2026 python:3.13-slim-trixie example did) is not the only option, though.
(a) Raspberry Pi's public apt repo (archive.raspberrypi.com) ships these packages for bookworm and trixie, arm64 and armhf, and can be added inside a debian:bookworm/trixie image:
- liblgpio1 / liblgpio-dev / python3-lgpio 0.2.2-1~rpt1(+trixie)
- python3-gpiozero 2.0.1-0+rpt1(+trixie)
These packages are built for Debian's /usr/bin/python3, not for the /usr/local Python of the official python:* images.
(b) Ubuntu, which is Debian-based, ships liblgpio1 and python3-lgpio in universe for amd64, arm64 and armhf:
- jammy 0.1.6.1
- noble and questing 0.2.0.0
- resolute 26.04: present, version not captured

https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/master/daemon/pkg/oci/defaults.go:
- lines 84–87: Destination "/sys", Type "sysfs", Options {"nosuid","noexec","nodev","ro"}.
- Masked paths under /sys: only "/sys/devices/virtual/powercap" (line 206), "/sys/firmware" (207) and per-CPU "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu%d/thermal_throttle" (213).
Podman (https://github.com/containers/podman/blob/main/pkg/specgen/generate/oci_linux.go):
- Non-privileged containers keep the generator's read-only sysfs.
- When a new sysfs cannot be mounted (host netns with rootless or userns), Podman bind-mounts host /sys with {"rprivate","nosuid","noexec","nodev","ro","rbind"}. Only privileged containers get rw.
So /sys/bus/w1/devices is visible read-only in both runtimes. w1 is not network-namespaced. This is still a code-level conclusion, not tested on hardware. AppArmor is covered by C41.

The sub-claims checked in this chunk hold:
- The kernel side (w1-gpio overlay, SPI mux, persist/strict_gpiod, gpiochip numbering) lives on the host.
- Containers see /sys read-only (C39) and need explicit --device plus a numeric GID.
- lgpio/gpiozero need extra image build steps (C21, C23, C24).
- Pi 5 chip renumbering (C04) affects the container's device map, not just the app.
Not verified: 'gpio group/udev rules present on Raspberry Pi OS only'. Other distros (e.g. Ubuntu for Pi) may ship their own gpiochip group rule; one 2026 blog shows root:gpio on Ubuntu, but this is unconfirmed.
Additional host steps the list omits:
- Docker: the docker service must be enabled at boot.
- Rootless Podman: `loginctl enable-linger` and a user-manager restart after joining gpio (C37).
- If the HAL selects the gpiochip by label (needed because of C04), a static --device list cannot follow renumbering. The chip must be resolved on the host when the container starts, or all /dev/gpiochip* nodes passed in.

missed: Non-root native systemd deployment hits the lgpio FIFO problem too, not just containers. systemd's default WorkingDirectory is '/', so `import lgpio` creates the FIFO at '//.lgd-nfy0' and fails for a non-root User= (joan2937/lg issue #22). The native unit needs a writable WorkingDirectory=, or e.g. RuntimeDirectory=brewberrypi plus Environment=LG_WD=/run/brewberrypi. Because lgpio chdir()s into LG_WD at import, the app must use absolute paths. Two lgpio processes sharing a directory unlink each other's FIFOs (issue #12).

The Raspberry Pi apt python3-gpiozero (2.0.1-0+rpt1, still current in bookworm and trixie) still ignores LGPIOFactory(chip=N); its patch only adds the /dev/gpiochip4 existence check. Only PyPI 2.0.1.post3 honours chip=. On a renumbered Pi 5 kernel (pinctrl-rp1 = gpiochip15, C04), the apt gpiozero cannot be pointed at the right chip, and post3's auto-detect falls back to chip 0, which is missing. So the BrewberryPi HAL needs label-based chip discovery passed explicitly as chip=N, which requires the PyPI post3 build, or its own gpiod/lgpio HAL.

gpiozero 2.0.1.post1 and post2 are yanked on PyPI (reason 'bug'). Unpinned or `>=2.0.1` installs now get post3. Only exact pins or lock files from 2026-07-25..27 can still pull the broken builds. Use GPIOZERO_PIN_FACTORY=lgpio so that any lgpio failure (missing chip, unwritable FIFO dir, wrong chip number) is loud instead of a silent fallback to RPiGPIO/native. Silent fallback is a safety issue for the heater relay.

An Ubuntu base image, or a Debian image with archive.raspberrypi.com added, can apt-install lgpio and gpiozero for arm64 and armhf without swig or a compiler. These packages bind to the distro's /usr/bin/python3: Ubuntu noble has Python 3.12; Raspberry Pi trixie packages target Debian's 3.13. They therefore suit a debian/ubuntu base image, not the official python:* images. This reduces the C23/C24 build burden for container images.

Pi 5 gpiochip renumbering is not limited to the 6.12.96 Bookworm regression. Non-Raspberry-Pi-OS kernels (e.g. WLAN Pi's 7.1.13/7.2.7-2712) also put pinctrl-rp1 at gpiochip15, and the /dev/gpiochip4 symlink exists only when RP1 is gpiochip0. A robust deployment must resolve the header chip by label (pinctrl-rp1 / pinctrl-bcm2711 / pinctrl-bcm2835). In a container that means either a host-side start hook that maps the resolved node, e.g. `--device /dev/gpiochipN:/dev/gpiochip0`, or passing every gpiochip node. A fixed `--device /dev/gpiochip0` makes the container fail to start; native code fails at runtime.
lgpio's prebuilt manylinux wheels require glibc >= 2.34 and none exist for musl. Alpine images and Raspberry Pi OS Bullseye (glibc 2.31) always build from source, even on Python <= 3.12.
